candidates.attacker_control: A different local (unprivileged) user on the same multi-user POSIX host can list the shared temp directory (e.g. /tmp) and create/delete entries there. The attacker does not control test inputs, but observes the junitNNNN.tmp placeholder created at line 237 and can pre-create the derived junitNNNN directory (or otherwise race line 242) before the rule executes its mkdir. Data written underneath the rule's folder by the test (or by code under test) is placed there by the victim, not the attacker.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: recursiveDelete (294-309) deletes a file before recursing so symlinks are not followed, limiting symlink-based deletion abuse; newFolder rejects absolute paths (194-198); names generated by File.createTempFile are randomized so blind pre-creation is infeasible, meaning the race requires observing the shared directory; newFile(String)/newFolder(String) build paths from getRoot() (lines 154, 205); the whole behaviour requires a shared temp directory and a permissive umask, so single-user or per-user-tempdir environments are unaffected; no other file-writing or permission-relevant API was found in main sources (searches for Files., PosixFilePermission, setReadable/setWritable/setExecutable, Runtime.exec, ProcessBuilder, Socket returned no main-source file-handling sinks besides TemporaryFolder, MaxHistory and BaseTestRunner preferences).
candidates.impact: Local information disclosure: on a shared temp directory with a typical umask, the rule's directory (0755) and files created under it (0644) are listable/readable by other local users while the test runs, leaking any test data stored there. With a permissive umask the directory can be world-writable, allowing other users to add, replace or remove entries (tampering/flakiness). The observable placeholder plus non-atomic mkdir also lets a local user pre-create the derived name, forcing repeated retries and potentially an IOException after the retry budget, i.e. local denial of service against the test run. This is a local-only, disclosure/integrity issue, not remote code execution.
candidates.prerequisites: TemporaryFolder used with the default constructor (or a shared/world-traversable parent folder supplied to the builder/constructor) on a POSIX multi-user host whose java.io.tmpdir is shared; process umask that leaves group/other read+execute (typical 022) for disclosure, or group/other write (e.g. 000) for modification; test or code under test writes sensitive data (credentials, tokens, fixtures) into the folder; attacker has local access. Systems with per-user temp directories (macOS, Windows) or single-user hosts are not affected in the same way.
candidates.root_cause: TemporaryFolder.create() delegates to createTemporaryFolderIn(), which reserves a name with File.createTempFile(TMP_PREFIX, ".tmp", parentFolder) (line 237), strips the ".tmp" suffix, and then creates the directory with createdFolder.mkdir() (line 242). All creation paths rely on java.io.File APIs (File.createTempFile, File.mkdir, File.mkdirs, File.createNewFile) which create entries with the process umask; no code sets owner-only permissions, and the source tree contains no java.nio.file.Files / PosixFilePermission / setReadable/setWritable/setExecutable usage at all (verified by search). With the default constructor parentFolder is null, so the root is created in the shared system temp directory; the placeholder file name is observable there, exposing the directory name that line 242 will create, and the mkdir is not atomic with respect to other users.
candidates.title: TemporaryFolder creates its temporary directory/files with umask-default permissions in the shared temp directory (local disclosure, race)
candidates.trace: Test method execution wraps @Rule statements (BlockJUnit4ClassRunner.methodBlock -> RuleContainer.apply) -> ExternalResource.apply (ExternalResource.java:42-67) -> TemporaryFolder.before() (TemporaryFolder.java:131-134) -> create() (146-148) -> createTemporaryFolderIn() (232-251). At 237 File.createTempFile creates the world-listable placeholder in the shared temp dir; at 240-242 the placeholder name minus ".tmp" is turned into a File and created via mkdir() with umask defaults. Tests then obtain the path via getRoot() (256-262) and create more entries with newFile()/newFile(String)/newFolder(String...) (153-223), which likewise use createTempFile/createNewFile/mkdirs with umask defaults. Deletion happens later via delete() -> tryDelete() -> recursiveDelete() (271-309). No permission-restriction call exists anywhere on this path or in the source tree.
candidates.unverified: The actual runtime directory/file modes depend on the host OS and umask; this was not executed or measured. It is not established that permission hardening is the exact change the maintainers intended for this snapshot, or that this is the only issue the snapshot contains. Files not read in depth (Assert.java, junit.framework.*, experimental theories/categories/parameterized internals, JUnit38ClassRunner, matchers) were only spot-checked or searched, so an injected/logic defect there cannot be fully excluded.
candidates.weakness_type: Insecure temporary file/directory creation: permissions inherited from umask with no owner-only hardening, plus non-atomic name-based directory creation (local information disclosure / TOCTOU)

coverage_summary: Source scope reported 279 files (no binary exclusions, no sensitive-name exclusions; same filters for B0 and P1), and the P1 relation index reports complete syntactic coverage of all 279 files (0 missing) with 2,128 symbols, 3,428 calls and 4,272 edges, but no data-flow or reachability analysis. I read the TemporaryFolder implementation in full and the surrounding rule plumbing (ExternalResource, RunRules, RuleContainer, RunBefores, RunAfters, FailOnTimeout), the runner core (ParentRunner full, BlockJUnit4ClassRunner 1-300, TestClass 1-200, MethodSorter full), request/description/notification paths (Request, JUnitCommandLineParseResult, FilterFactories, Classes, Description 240-327, RunNotifier 1-120, ErrorReportingRunner), the experimental max path (MaxHistory full, MaxCore 1-120), JUnit3 compatibility paths (BaseTestRunner 1-250, ActiveTestSuite, MethodRoadie 1-80, textui TestRunner 100-160) and Throwables 1-120, plus targeted searches across the whole tree for file/process/network/crypto/permission/deserialization sinks (Runtime.exec, ProcessBuilder, Socket, MessageDigest, Files., PosixFilePermission, setReadable/setExecutable, ObjectInputStream, Class.forName, System.getProperty/getenv, mkdir, createNewFile, new File). Uninspected-in-depth areas: Assert.java, junit.framework.*, experimental theories/categories/parameterized internals, matchers, JUnit38ClassRunner, ResultPrinter/TextListener, validator and management internals.
limitations: No build, tests, or any execution was performed; directory/file permission behaviour is reasoned from the java.io.File APIs and the absence of permission-hardening calls, not measured.
The P1 index is syntactic only (declarations/calls/containment/hints); its 5 facts are navigation hints, not findings, and I verified every cited line against source text myself.
The severity and applicability depend on deployment details that source cannot show: OS, umask, whether java.io.tmpdir is shared, and whether tests store sensitive data in the folder.

Large parts of the tree were only spot-checked or searched (Assert, junit.framework.*, theories/categories/parameterized internals, matchers, JUnit38ClassRunner), so a defect injected in those areas cannot be fully excluded.
I did not use or assume any CVE/ground-truth/patch information; the snapshot's version string and absent later release notes were treated only as context.
The candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability; no runtime confirmation exists.

rejected_leads.lead: MaxHistory.readHistory deserializes a MaxHistory object from a Java ObjectInputStream (src/main/java/org/junit/experimental/max/MaxHistory.java:45-62; save at 77-87).
rejected_leads.reason: A Java-deserialization gadget path requires attacker write access to the history file (chosen by the embedding application through MaxCore.storedLocally/forFolder) before it is read, and the object is cast to MaxHistory. No attacker-controlled input reaches this path in the library itself, and the design is pre-existing/unchanged rather than a locally fixable defect; left as an unconfirmed secondary lead, not a candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: FailOnTimeout spawns a daemon 'Time-limited test' thread per timed test and calls ThreadGroup.destroy() (src/main/java/org/junit/internal/runners/statements/FailOnTimeout.java:119-146), with lookForStuckThread enumerating threads.
rejected_leads.reason: Thread/resource exhaustion concerns exist, but there is no attacker-controlled input or trust boundary in the library, and the timeout thread behaviour is intentional (thread is daemon, interrupt is attempted, destroy exceptions are swallowed); insufficient security impact to prefer over the TemporaryFolder candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Classes.getClass uses Class.forName(className, true, contextClassLoader) (src/main/java/org/junit/internal/Classes.java:40-43) and FilterFactories/JUnitCommandLineParseResult instantiate classes named on the command line (FilterFactories.java:21-81).
rejected_leads.reason: Class initialization/instantiation from user-supplied names is a documented CLI feature; an attacker who can supply the runner arguments and classpath already controls the process, so this is not a privilege boundary crossing.

rejected_leads.lead: TemporaryFolder.newFolder(String...) only rejects absolute paths and allows '..' components (TemporaryFolder.java:184-223).
rejected_leads.reason: The caller is the test code itself (already trusted with process privileges), so traversal outside the rule root is a robustness quirk rather than an escalation; the deletion path still refuses to follow symlinks.
Local preference read of a properties file; no sensitive data handling or attacker-controlled path, and IOException/SecurityException are ignored.

summary: This is a JUnit 4 source snapshot (pom version 4.14-SNAPSHOT; no tests, docs and site resources included). The strongest source-evidenced candidate is the TemporaryFolder rule: it creates its root directory and child files/directories using java.io.File creation methods (File.createTempFile, mkdir, mkdirs, createNewFile) that apply the process umask and are never tightened with any permission API. When the default constructor is used, the rule's root is created inside the shared system temp directory (java.io.tmpdir), and the directory name is derived from an observable ".tmp" placeholder, so another local user can read test data placed in the folder (owner-only permissions are never applied) and can race the subsequent mkdir by pre-creating the derived name. Secondary areas reviewed (runner plumbing, class loading, JUnit3 compatibility, experimental MaxCore/MaxHistory, statements/rules) showed no stronger attacker-reachable defect; the MaxHistory Java-deserialization path is a plausible but weaker, pre-existing design lead because it requires write access to the history file.
